title: Does Deterministic Generate–Validate–Repair Reduce Unsafe LLM‑Generated Network Changes? A Confirmatory Paired Study
abstract: We preregistered and executed a sealed paired confirmatory study (n = 200 intent→configuration tasks) to test whether a deterministic generate–validate–repair (GVR) pipeline that consults a deterministic NetOps validator reduces validator‑detected unsafe or semantically incorrect network changes relative to an LLM‑only pipeline. The run used a single hosted model (gpt‑5‑mini) with adapter‑enforced shared‑initial generation semantics and a primary deterministic validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5). Execution consumed 200 model calls (one shared initial generation per task); no repair calls were issued because every initial candidate passed the validator. Paired contingency: n11 = 200, n10 = 0, n01 = 0, n00 = 0; estimate of paired difference = 0.0; exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0; 95% bootstrap percentile CI = [0.0, 0.0] (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729). Because the baseline validator‑detected unsafe incidence was 0%, the preregistered ≥50% relative‑reduction hypothesis could not be meaningfully evaluated on this task bank. We report the sealed design, execution accounting, representative examples, contamination‑check evidence (Mininet holdout = 10% → 20 tasks; contamination summary records zero disagreements), and an artifact‑grounded discussion of operational implications and threats to validity (preregistration id: cnsms2026-gvr-effectiveness-02).

sections.introduction:
Automating intent→configuration translation with generative models promises operational productivity gains but creates exposure to incorrect or unsafe changes that can cause outages, policy violations, or degraded service. Prior proposals therefore combine LLM generation with deterministic validators and repair loops (generate–validate–repair, GVR) to detect and correct unsafe candidates before application. However, the operational value of automated repairs depends on the baseline prevalence of validator‑detectable failures and on validator coverage. We ask: does a deterministic GVR pipeline materially reduce the incidence of deterministic‑validator‑detected unsafe or semantically incorrect network changes compared to an LLM‑only pipeline on a curated 200‑task intent→configuration bank?

Contributions. (1) A sealed, preregistered paired confirmatory design (n = 200) that enforces shared‑initial generation semantics across conditions and limits repair calls to one per task; (2) a fully archived autonomous execution and deterministic reconciliation with concrete accounting (model_calls_used = 200, repair_calls = 0); (3) an honest, artifact‑grounded null/degenerate confirmatory outcome and interpretation showing when automated repair is conditionally useful, together with explicit reproducibility notes and operational recommendations.
sections.related_work: Large language models exhibit factual errors and prompt sensitivity across domains; mitigation strategies include grounding (RAG), verifier‑assisted repair, and bounded/guarded agent architectures. Prototype NetOps systems demonstrate intent→configuration feasibility but often lack instrumented failure‑rate evaluations in production‑like settings. Red‑team and configuration‑brittleness studies show agent/tool descriptions and tool‑chaining can change safety outcomes materially. These prior findings motivate preregistered, externally auditable evaluations that isolate the marginal effect of adding deterministic repair for a fixed model, prompt policy, and validator: is repair redundant when baseline generation already satisfies validator constraints, or does it provide measurable risk reduction? Our study situates itself among generator→validator→repair proposals and external‑evaluation critiques by measuring the planned estimand (paired success rate difference) under tightly controlled, archived conditions.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and inferential plan. The study (cnsms2026-gvr-effectiveness-02) froze a paired design with n = 200 tasks, a single pre‑registered primary test (exact McNemar two‑sided, α = 0.05), and a model‑call cap of 400 (initial generation 1 call per task plus up to 1 repair call per failing candidate). The primary estimand was the paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline; primary inference used an exact McNemar test and bootstrap percentile CIs (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729) per the preregistered analysis_plan. All design choices, stopping rules, and the repair budget were preregistered; no design changes occurred post‑lock.

Task bank and validators. We used a curated, machine‑checkable intent→configuration bank of 200 tasks spanning four topology clusters (enterprise, campus, datacenter, edge; 50 tasks each). Each task encodes the initial and expected final states, workflow constraints (e.g., make‑before‑break, all‑down‑before‑mtu‑change), and an explicit required_sequence. The primary deterministic checker was deterministic_netops_validator_v5, which enforces intent/constraint checks and reports pass/fail plus structured diagnostics. A Mininet‑based data‑plane emulator was preregistered as a secondary disagreement detector applied to a randomized 10% holdout (20 tasks) to detect validator–emulator mismatches; the preregistered holdout fraction and contamination artifact are recorded in the execution bundle and the analysis/contamination_summary.csv shows zero disagreement flags.

Model, generation semantics, and adapter enforcement. The experiments used one hosted model (declared: gpt‑5‑mini) invoked through the hosted_netops_gvr_v1 adapter. Crucially, the adapter enforced shared_initial generation semantics: for each task the system produced a single initial candidate (temperature = 0 policy; one API call) which was then reused for both baseline (LLM‑only) and guarded (GVR) conditions. The adapter accounted for hosted_model_call_event_count = 200 and stage_counts = {shared_initial_generation: 200} (execution manifest). The shared‑initial policy was a preregistered conservative design intended to isolate the effect of applying a validator+repair to the same generated candidate; it also deterministically removes per‑condition sampling variance, so if the initial candidate passes the validator there is no opportunity for repair under the prescribed single‑repair budget.

Repair policy and contamination handling. Per the preregistration, when deterministic_netops_validator_v5 reports violations, the adapter issues one automated repair prompt to the same LLM and then re‑validates. The contamination_plan specified deterministic exclusion of tasks where primary validator vs emulator disagree; sensitivity analyses were also preregistered to examine the impact of including flagged tasks as failures or successes. The missingness_plan and exclusion rules are archived and were executed deterministically; execution artifacts record 0 failed episodes and 0 exclusions for the confirmatory sample.
sections.results:
Execution accounting. The autonomous run completed the planned paired sample: completed_episode_count = 400 (200 shared initial generation events reused across conditions), complete_pair_count = 200, model_calls_used = 200 (no repair calls consumed), failed_episode_count = 0. Condition summaries (analysis/condition_summary.csv) record baseline successes = 200/200 and guarded successes = 200/200 (success_rate = 1.0 for both). The paired contingency table (analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv) is n11 = 200, n10 = 0, n01 = 0, n00 = 0.

Primary inferential result. With the observed contingency, the paired difference estimate = 0.0. The exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0; the bootstrap percentile 95% CI (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729) = [0.0, 0.0]. Because there are zero discordant pairs, the preregistered hypothesis (≥50% relative reduction in validator‑detected unsafe changes) is logically untestable on this sample: there were no baseline failures for GVR to reduce. The analysis artifacts (analysis/results.json and paired tables) and deterministic reconciliation logs record these numbers and the bootstrap parameters.

Repair activity and contamination checks. No initial candidate failed the primary validator, therefore the GVR pipeline applied zero repair prompts and incurred zero repair‑call cost. The preregistered Mininet holdout (10% → 20 tasks) executed as recorded; analysis/contamination_summary.csv records no validator–emulator disagreement flags. The execution manifest nonetheless contains a reproducibility gap: the explicit randomized holdout selection seed for the Mininet contamination check is not present as a labeled artifact, which prevents deterministic reconstruction of the exact holdout selection even though the contamination artifact reports zero disagreements.

Representative example. A representative task (pair‑000001) required migrating edge1 to VLAN 30 and MTU 1600 using a shutdown→configure→restore workflow. The shared initial candidate (and both condition responses) produced the four ordered commands that satisfied the task constraints and passed deterministic_netops_validator_v5; validator traces record valid = true and violation_count = 0 for that episode. Several additional representative task artifacts (tasks 000002–000006) show identical patterns: generated candidate → validator pass → no repair.
sections.discussion:
Interpretation and conditionality. The observed null/degenerate confirmatory outcome shows a simple logical point: when the chosen model, prompt policy, and adapter produce validator‑passing candidates for all tasks in a workload, an automated repair step cannot reduce validator‑detected failures. This does not imply that GVR is useless in general; rather, it highlights that GVR's marginal operational benefit is conditional on baseline failure prevalence and on validator coverage. If baseline validator failure prevalence is near zero for the evaluated workload, resources allocated to automated repair yield no measured benefit for validator‑detected error rates.

Why the null occurred in this run. Artifact‑grounded explanations include: (1) prompt policy and shared_initial semantics produced candidates already satisfying the encoded intent constraints; (2) the curated task bank encodes workflows that map cleanly to validator checks and therefore may be biased toward validator‑satisfiable solutions; (3) the primary validator enforces task‑bank‑encoded constraints but may not model certain real device or vendor idiosyncrasies that would appear only in end‑to‑end deployments; and (4) the single repair budget combined with shared_initial semantics removes per‑condition resampling as a pathway to produce alternative candidates that might trigger repair sequences.

Operational implications. Practitioners should measure baseline validator failure prevalence on representative workloads before investing in automated repair automation: when baseline failure rates are low, efforts are better spent extending validator fidelity (emulator/real‑device checks), adversarial testing, multi‑model sampling, or human‑in‑the‑loop approvals. Where baseline failures are non‑negligible, GVR can reduce validator‑detected issues, but the realized benefit will depend on repair budget, repair prompt engineering, and validator completeness. Additionally, adversarial vectors (tool‑description injection, cross‑tool ambiguity) documented in red‑team studies remain operational threats that a nominal GVR loop may not fully mitigate.

Reproducibility and reported gap. All key execution artifacts (model‑call logs, validator traces, paired contingency tables, bootstrap seeds) are archived. One reproducibility gap remains: the labeled artifact for the randomized Mininet holdout selection seed is absent, preventing exact reconstruction of the holdout sampling despite the contamination summary reporting zero disagreements. We report this gap transparently and include the analysis/contamination_summary.csv evidence that no disagreements were observed in the executed holdout.

Threats to validity. Internal validity is protected by preregistration and deterministic adapter enforcement, but the shared_initial design trades generality for control: it isolates the validator/repair effect on a fixed candidate but does not measure benefits obtainable by re‑sampling or by multi‑attempt generation. Construct validity is limited by primary validator coverage; end‑to‑end emulator or real‑device behaviors may reveal failures the validator misses. External validity is restricted by single‑model evaluation (gpt‑5‑mini), single sampling policy, and a curated task bank that may not reflect adversarial or production distributions. Conclusion validity is limited because the primary confirmatory test is trivially uninformative when discordant pairs are zero; however, reporting the null outcome and its cause is itself an important operational datum.
sections.conclusion: We preregistered and ran a sealed paired study comparing LLM‑only generation to a deterministic GVR pipeline on 200 NetOps intent→configuration tasks using gpt‑5‑mini and deterministic_netops_validator_v5. Both pipelines produced validator‑passing configurations for every task (n11 = 200, no discordant pairs). The preregistered hypothesis of a ≥50% relative reduction in validator‑detected unsafe changes is not testable on this task bank because the baseline failure rate was 0%. The result is narrowly scoped: GVR reduces validator‑detected failures only in workloads where baseline validator failures occur or where validators can expose additional failure modes; extending evaluations to adversarial draws, multi‑model sampling, larger repair budgets, and emulator/real‑device verification is necessary to measure practical GVR value in production NetOps. All execution artifacts, logs, and analysis outputs are archived in the execution bundle for independent inspection.

disclosure_statement: Disclosure (mandatory). This study executed under the autonomous post‑lock preregistration cnsms2026-gvr-effectiveness-02 and used the hosted model declared as gpt‑5‑mini (provider label: openai_responses) invoked via the hosted_netops_gvr_v1 adapter family. The exact initial master prompt is archived at provenance/master_prompt.txt (SHA‑256: 1872df1e1805d2d96940456ca016bd665d1d5196add77f5acdf1582bb39b15ba). Topic constraints: the human Research Director limited the study to Generative AI and LLMs for NetOps focusing on safety/reliability of generated network changes. Frameworks and tools: code and experiment orchestration used the hosted_netops_gvr_v1 framework and the deterministic task generator (deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5). The primary deterministic validator was deterministic_netops_validator_v5 (intent/constraint checks). A Mininet‑based emulator served as the preregistered secondary disagreement detector applied to a randomized 10% holdout (20 tasks). Preregistration and freeze: the experimental plan (estimand, sample size n = 200, paired design, stopping rules, max model calls = 400, repair call budget = 1 per task, shared‑initial generation semantics) was frozen before any model calls. Autonomous execution and artifacts: the run executed autonomously under the frozen plan; model calls, prompts, seeds, validator traces, emulator traces, logs, and the artifact manifest are archived in the execution bundle. Model‑call budget and usage: 200 model calls were used (one shared initial generation per task); up to 200 repair calls were allowed but none were applied because initial candidates passed the validator. Human involvement: the human Research Director selected the topic family and pre‑lock constraints; no human manual editing or selective rewriting of technical manuscript content occurred after the autonomy lock. Deviations and restarts: no post‑preregistration design changes or technical restarts occurred. Known reproducibility gap: the explicit randomized holdout selection seed used for the Mininet contamination check is not present as a labeled artifact in the archived bundle; this absence prevents deterministic reconstruction of the exact holdout selection despite the contamination summary reporting no disagreements. The master prompt archive reference above is the immutable prompt required by the track.
limitations: Task‑bank scope: the confirmatory sample used a curated synthetic/public intent→configuration bank (n = 200); results therefore reflect this bank and may not generalize to broader production workloads or adversarial distributions.

Single‑model and shared‑initial setting: only gpt‑5‑mini (hosted) with adapter‑enforced shared‑initial generation was tested (execution artifacts record hosted_model_call_event_count = 200 and stage_counts shared_initial_generation = 200). Outcomes may differ across model families, independent per‑condition sampling, nonzero temperature sampling, or larger repair budgets.

Validator coverage and oracle limitations: the primary deterministic validator enforces a defined set of syntax/intent constraints; validators can fail to capture real device idiosyncrasies, vendor‑specific behaviors, or emergent failure modes detectable only by end‑to‑end deployment.

Adversarial robustness untested: this confirmatory run did not include active adversarial injection or red‑team tool‑description attacks; prior audits indicate such vectors can bypass naive defenses and remain a separate concern.

Reproducibility gap for contamination check: the randomized holdout selection seed for the Mininet contamination check is absent from the labeled artifacts, preventing exact reconstruction of the holdout selection.

Single repair budget: the GVR pipeline allowed at most one automated repair prompt per task; multi‑step repair strategies, different repair budgets, or human‑in‑the‑loop approvals were not exercised here.
